questions.learningObjective: find a coterminal angle in a standard interval
questions.stem: A propeller spins backward through an angle of minus 750 degrees. What coterminal angle in degrees lies between 0 and 360?
questions.explanation: Coterminal angles differ by whole turns of 360 degrees, so add 360 to minus 750 to get minus 390, add it once more to get minus 30, and add it a final time to reach 330, which lies between 0 and 360. Counting turns from the positive direction also works: minus 750 degrees is minus 750 plus 720 minus 30, that is two full turns plus minus 30 degrees, and minus 30 degrees is coterminal with 330 degrees. Either bookkeeping lands on the same terminal side, which is all coterminality means.
questions.hint: Add 360 repeatedly until the measure is nonnegative and under 360.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Steps for converting degrees to radians
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of a degree-to-radian conversion
questions.stem: Put these steps in the order that correctly converts an angle measured in degrees into radians.

options.text: Write the degree measure as a fraction over 180 so the half-turn ratio is visible
Multiply that fraction by pi, since 180 degrees equals pi radians
Cancel the degree units so only the radian measure remains
Reduce the resulting fraction so numerator and denominator share no factor
Check the answer by converting it back to degrees with 180 over pi

questions.explanation: The order is a chain of dependencies rather than of taste. Writing the measure over 180 has to come first because the half-turn ratio is the whole conversion, and nothing can be multiplied until it is on the page. Multiplying by pi follows at once, and cancelling the degree units follows the multiplication, because the units only cancel once both factors are present. Reduction waits for cancellation, since a factor chosen before the units are gone may not survive. The back-check comes last because it needs a finished radian value, and it is the cheapest way to catch an inverted factor: converting back must return the original degree measure.
questions.hint: Start by writing the degree measure over 180, then attach pi and simplify.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain the proportional basis of the degree-radian conversion
questions.stem: Explain why multiplying a degree measure by pi over 180 converts it to radians, and why the same angle can carry two different numbers.

answer.exemplar: The two scales share one fixed relationship: a half turn is 180 degrees and the same half turn is pi radians, so for any given angle the pair (degree number, radian number) is proportional, and the constant of proportionality is pi over 180. Writing an angle of D degrees as the fraction D over 180 of a half turn, and knowing that half turn equals pi radians, produces D times pi over 180 directly, so the factor is not a rule to memorize but a restatement of what the two scales mean by half a rotation. The same angle carries two numbers because a number without a scale is meaningless; 1.5708 radians and 90 degrees name the identical turn in two units, exactly as the same length can be 1 metre or 100 centimetres. The two scales are locked by pi, so every correct conversion must pass through pi, and any conversion that does not mention pi is inventing a new scale. The conversion only scales, never shifts, because both scales start at the same zero and mark the same direction, so an answer that adds or subtracts a constant, or that drops a sign, is breaking the structure rather than using it.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names the shared half-turn relationship, derives the factor pi/180 as D/180 of a half turn, and explains the two-number phenomenon with a units analogy before noting that the factor is a pure scaling with no shifting.
questions.hint: Start from the fact that 180 degrees and pi radians both describe a half turn.

The student lost a factor of ten, most likely by reading 1260 over 6 as 126 over 6, and the tell-tale test is size: 7*pi over 6 is a third-quadrant angle just past 180 degrees, so an answer in the twenties cannot be right. The reciprocal-factor option points the conversion the wrong way, and the 2100 option invents a place-value rule that never appears in division.
questions.hint: The pi cancels, leaving 7 times 180 divided by 6.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: convert a degree measure into an approximate radian measure
questions.stem: A roof rafter meets the horizontal at 160 degrees. Express that angle in radians, to six decimal places.
questions.explanation: Multiply 160 by pi over 180 to get 160 times pi over 180, and since both divide by 20, the exact measure is 8 times pi over 9, about 2.792527. A second route agrees: 160 degrees is 20 degrees short of the straight line, which is pi over 9 short of pi, and pi minus pi over 9 is 8 pi over 9. The result sits between pi over 2 and pi, as an obtuse angle in the second quadrant must.
questions.hint: Reduce 160 over 180 by dividing both by 20.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: True statements about the two scales
questions.learningObjective: evaluate claims relating radian and degree measures
questions.stem: Which two statements about degrees and radians are true? Select both.

options.text: An angle of 1 radian is larger than an angle of 1 degree
An angle of 3 radians is smaller than an angle of 3*pi radians
An angle of pi radians is 60 degrees, because pi over 3 radians is 60 degrees
options.misconception: scales the pi over 3 benchmark by 3 degrees instead of by a factor of 3 radians

options.text: The radian measure of an angle depends on the radius of the circle drawn
options.misconception: believes the scale is tied to the size of the circle rather than being a pure ratio

questions.explanation: Option A holds because 1 radian is about 57.3 degrees, which easily exceeds 1 degree, and this is the single most useful intuition about the two scales. Option B holds because both angles are expressed in radians and 3 is less than 3*pi, so the comparison needs no conversion at all. Option C fails because pi radians is 180 degrees, and scaling a benchmark means multiplying the whole 60 degrees by 3, to get 180, not 180. Option D fails because a radian is an arc length divided by a radius, so the radius cancels and the measure is independent of the circle drawn.
questions.hint: Convert when the scales differ, and compare directly when they already match.

options.text: 225 degrees, which is 5*pi/4 or about 3.926991 radians
225 degrees, which is 5*pi/2 or about 7.853982 radians
options.misconception: doubles the radian fraction when converting from degrees

options.misconception: adds an extra 15 degrees to the swing before converting

questions.explanation: The total swing is the change in heading, 135 minus negative 90, which is 135 plus 90, or 225 degrees. Converting, 225 times pi over 180 reduces because both divide by 45, leaving 5 times pi over 4, about 3.926991 radians. The doubled answer 5*pi over 2 would be a swing of 450 degrees, past a full turn, and the 45-degree answer forgets that a change from below zero to above zero spans both sides of the origin rather than their difference.
questions.hint: Subtract the starting heading from the ending heading, then multiply by pi/180.

options.text: pi/4

options.text: pi/2
options.misconception: doubles the angle up to the quarter turn of 90 degrees

questions.explanation: A quarter turn is 90 degrees, which is pi over 2 radians, and 45 degrees is half a quarter turn, so its measure is half of pi over 2, that is pi over 4. The halving chain continues cleanly: 22.5 degrees is pi over 8, and the nested halvings are the easiest way to recall the whole family. The 30 and 60 degree benchmarks live at pi over 6 and pi over 3, and pi over 2 is twice the target, since it is the quarter turn itself.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: convert a radian measure beyond a full turn into degrees
questions.stem: A steering wheel is turned through 12 times pi over 5 radians. Convert that rotation to degrees.
questions.explanation: Multiply 12 times pi over 5 by 180 over pi to get 12 times 180 over 5, and 180 over 5 is 36, so the rotation is 12 times 36, which is 432 degrees. The second route peels off the full turn first: 12*pi over 5 exceeds 2*pi, which is 10*pi over 5, by 2*pi over 5, and 2*pi over 5 is 72 degrees, so the total is 360 plus 72, again 432. Either way the wheel turns once all the way round plus a fifth more.
questions.hint: Compute 12 times 180 over 5; expect a value above 360.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: construct an argument that the two scales are locked by one constant
questions.stem: A friend insists that radians and degrees are unrelated numbers that happen to measure angles. Construct the argument that convinces them the two scales are locked by one constant, using at least two anchor angles as evidence.

answer.exemplar: The convincing move is to stop treating the two numbers as labels and start treating them as readings of one proportional relationship. Both scales begin at the same zero and mark the same direction of turn, and both mark a complete revolution, so for every angle the two scales must agree on the ratio of any two parts of the turn. Declare the half turn as the anchor: it is 180 degrees and it is pi radians, so degree number over radian number is 180 over pi for the half turn, and by proportionality that ratio holds at every angle, which fixes the conversion constants pi over 180 and 180 over pi. Anchor one is the quarter turn: 90 degrees and pi over 2 radians, and indeed 180 over pi times pi over 2 returns 90, while pi over 180 times 90 returns pi over 2. Anchor two is a sixth of a turn: 60 degrees and pi over 3 radians, and the same two constants convert between them, because 180 over pi times pi over 3 is 60 and pi over 180 times 60 is pi over 3. No third scale could share these anchors with different constants, since two fixed points already pin the line through the origin, and any conversion that is not a pure scaling by the constant would have to add or subtract something, which would break the agreement at zero. The friend's claim also fails a practical test: if the scales were unrelated, no chart could label the same angle once in degrees and once in radians, yet every diagram does exactly that without contradiction.

questions.explanation: A strong construction states the shared anchors, derives the fixed ratio 180 over pi, verifies it at two specific angles by converting in both directions, and argues that two anchors pin a line through the origin so no independent scale could agree.
questions.hint: Pick two angles whose degree and radian measures you know exactly, then show one constant converts between them both.
